content: The World Health Organization (WHO) South-East Asia Region has developed sodium benchmarks for packaged foods to address the rising consumption of high-sodium products in the region. These benchmarks, published in September 2023, aim to guide countries in reducing sodium levels in packaged foods, which are a significant contributor to dietary sodium intake. The benchmarks were established by reviewing global sodium targets and tailoring them to the dietary patterns and sodium sources specific to South-East Asia. The benchmarks were developed with input from technical experts, including researchers from The George Institute for Global Health in Australia and Wageningen University in the Netherlands, as well as national experts and WHO country offices. The process involved identifying priority food categories that contribute significantly to sodium intake, such as bread, bakery products, instant noodles, processed meats, and snacks. The benchmarks are designed to encourage food manufacturers to reformulate products with lower sodium levels. Interim sodium targets were established for certain food categories, allowing gradual reductions over a four-year period. For example, the median sodium content of products like nuts, seeds, and kernels was used to set interim targets, with further reductions planned after compliance reviews. New subcategories were created for specific products, such as papads, seafood-based snacks, and instant noodles with seasoning, to address variations in sodium content and consumption patterns. These subcategories reflect the unique dietary habits of the region and provide more precise targets for sodium reduction. The benchmarks also emphasize the importance of equitable sodium reduction policies. Unlike front-of-pack labeling (FoPL) systems, which rely on consumer interpretation, sodium reformulation targets apply to the entire food supply, benefiting all consumers regardless of socioeconomic status or education level. Countries in the region are encouraged to adapt the benchmarks to their specific contexts by collecting data on commonly consumed products and their sodium content. Additionally, countries may consider implementing mandatory sodium targets, with support provided to small and medium enterprises to achieve compliance. The South-East Asia Region sodium benchmarks are a living document and will be updated over time as dietary patterns and sodium sources evolve.
